Suppose \(f(c)=0\). Then \(P(c,y)\) gives
\[
c y f(y^2)=0\qquad(\forall y).
\]
If \(c\ne0\), then \(f(u)=0\) for every \(u>0\). For any \(x<0\), taking \(y>0\) with \(y^2\ne-x\) in \(P(x,y)\) yields \(f(yf(x))=0\). Consequently \(f(x)\ge0\): indeed, if \(f(x)<0\), varying such positive \(y\) would make every negative number a zero of \(f\), forcing \(f\equiv0\).

Now fix \(x<0\). Taking \(y=\sqrt{-x}\) in \(P(x,y)\) gives
\[
f(f(x)-x)=0.
\]
Since \(f(x)\ge0\), we have \(f(x)-x>0\), which is consistent with the established positive zeros. Instead take any \(y<0\) with \(y^2\ne-x\). Since \(y^2+f(x)>0\), the right side of \(P(x,y)\) is zero, so \(f(yf(x))=0\). If \(f(x)>0\), varying negative \(y\) again makes every negative number a zero, contradicting \(f\not\equiv0\). Hence \(f(x)=0\). Thus \(f\equiv0\), a contradiction. Therefore every zero is \(0\).

For \(x<0\), choose \(y=\sqrt{-x}\). Then \(P(x,y)\) gives \(f(f(x)-x)=0\), so the uniqueness of the zero implies \(f(x)=x\).

\[
(y^2-1)(-y)=-y f(y^2-1),
\]
hence \(f(t)=t\). Therefore
\[
\boxed{f\equiv0\quad\text{or}\quad f(x)=x\ \text{for all }x\in\mathbb R.}
